from fractions import Fraction as Q

def eta(a,b):
 return 1-b/a if b<a else ((b-a)/(1-a) if b>a else Q(0))
def metrics(x1,x2):
 v1,v2=9*x1,Q(7,3)*x2-Q(1,6)
 u0=min(Q(7,15)*eta(x1,x2),Q(3,10)*eta(x2,x1))
 u1=min(Q(1,5)*eta(v1,v2),Q(1,30)*eta(v2,v1))
 e=Q(3,10)*x1+Q(7,15)*x2+Q(1,30)*v1+Q(1,5)*v2
 return u0+u1,e
A=metrics(Q(0),Q(1,14))
B=metrics(Q(1,14),Q(1,14))
C=metrics(Q(1,36),Q(1,14))
print('Exact feasible (unfairness,error) pairs:')
for label,pair in [('A',A),('B',B),('C',C)]: print(label,tuple(map(str,pair)),tuple(map(float,pair)))
beta=(B[1]-A[1])/(B[1]-A[1]+A[0]-B[0])
print('A/B weighted-objective crossing beta:',beta)
print('At crossing, objective A:', beta*A[0]+(1-beta)*A[1],'; objective C:',beta*C[0]+(1-beta)*C[1])
print('Rare-label example: equal group weights, prevalence delta, FNR .1 and .2, FPR zero; unfairness/delta =', min(Q(1,2)*eta(Q(1,10),Q(1,5)),Q(1,2)*eta(Q(1,5),Q(1,10))))
print('Lemma 4: tau_beta(x,x/2)=beta/2+(1-beta)*(1-x/2); derivative magnitude=(1-beta)/2, while D(0,1,0,1/2)=0.')
PY"

strengths: Auditing classifiers from aggregate statistics is an important, well-motivated problem. The formulation clearly identifies what information is available and provides useful connections between label proportions, fairness, and classification error.

The mixture-based unfairness definition has a precise interpretation as a minimum contamination mass. Its decomposition across true labels, monotonicity under coarsening predicted labels, and finite-candidate characterization for binary confusion matrices provide valuable structural insights.

The experiments cover numerous classifiers and several application domains. The multiclass initialization ablations support the usefulness of combining the greedy procedure with local optimization; several reported lower and upper bounds coincide or nearly coincide.

The manuscript acknowledges its relationship to the 2020 predecessor, discusses limitations when few subpopulations are available, and provides an implementation link. These support informed assessment and potential reproduction.
weaknesses: The binary approximation guarantee has a concrete mathematical gap. Lemma 4 bounds derivatives of τβ, but Appendix B only analyzes η and omits the error contribution. Set a=c=0, b=1, and d=1/2. For x in (0,1), the stated bound is zero, whereas τβ(x,x/2)=β/2+(1−β)(1−x/2) has derivative magnitude (1−β)/2. Consequently, the Lipschitz constants used by ArgMin1D do not establish Algorithm 2's advertised tolerance guarantee for β<1.

Several optimization formulas do not represent the stated discrepancy. Section 8.1 switches from diagonal probabilities to false-positive/false-negative rates but continues using τβ(a,b)=βη(a,b)+(1−β)(1−b); the error contribution should then involve b. Separately, the error terms in Equations (29) and (32) omit the population weights wgπg^y under the stated definition of Fy. These may be repairable formulation errors, but the implementation and affected results need checking before the computational claims are reproducible.

The claimed exact recovery of constrained trade-offs in Sections 8 and 8.3 is incorrect in general. Weighted scalarization can miss unsupported Pareto points. For example, take group weights (1/3,2/3), true-positive proportions (0.1,0.3), and predicted-positive proportions (0.1,0.35). Scalarized optima jump between (unfairness,error)=(0.03333,0.03333) and (0.02143,0.07619), while error 0.05 is compatible with unfairness 0.02929. The stated β-search would instead report 0.03333 as the minimum unfairness under that error cap. Valid supporting-line bounds or direct constrained optimization are needed.

Multiclass certification remains incomplete. Although Section 8.3 acknowledges that local optimization supplies only upper bounds on the minimum discrepancy, the aggregate-data experiments do not report corresponding certified lower bounds or optimization gaps. Furthermore, Sections 7.2.2 and 8.2 alter confusion probabilities or label proportions for numerical stability. Bounds for these modified inputs do not automatically certify the original problem; the assertion that existing sampling noise makes this harmless requires a perturbation argument or verification against the original constraints.

The claimed advantage for rare labels is overstated. If two equally weighted groups have disease prevalence δ, zero false-positive rates, and false-negative rates 0.1 and 0.2, Equation (6) gives unfairness δ/18, which vanishes with prevalence despite the doubled false-negative rate. Indeed, choosing the identity baseline shows unfairness≤error. Population weighting is a legitimate modeling choice, but it does not establish the claimed high sensitivity to rare-label disparities, and conditional absolute-rate differences need not vanish in this example.

The evidence for the new computational contributions is incomplete relative to the acknowledged 2020 binary work. There are no runtime/scaling comparisons establishing the benefit of the new binary search procedure, and the multiclass aggregate experiments test only β=1. Small instances with certified global solutions, optimization-gap measurements, and experiments with β<1 would substantially strengthen the contribution beyond the existing framework.

The biomedical applications do not establish that all aggregate quantities describe the same population and label event. State cancer incidence is not necessarily the prevalence of having cancer among Bing users during the query window. Such mismatches can generate apparent unfairness independently of classifier behavior. Section 5 briefly mentions uncertainty intervals, but the later nonlinear analyses do not propagate sampling uncertainty or assess sensitivity to these population assumptions.

Minor reporting errors also need correction. Figure 6 and its discussion invert the bound-to-true-value ratio: the stated true-unfairness/lower-bound ratio cannot have medians of 48% and 23%. This obscures the interpretation of the empirical tightness results.
